title: BMO Says Quantum Computing Can Help Banks Detect Risk
excerpt: BMO says it has demonstrated quantum utility in a machine learning application with the help of IBM quantum computers. As the bank said in a news
content:
BMO says it has demonstrated quantum utility in a machine learning application with the help of IBM quantum computers.

As the bank said in a news release Thursday (Nov. 19), this means the work was done “reliably at a scale beyond what exact traditional computing methods can practically reproduce.”

The work examines how quantum computing might help artificial intelligence (AI) models identify which information is the most important in complex datasets, potentially allowing them to glean useful insights with less data than traditional strategies, BMO added.

“Over time, that capability could have applications across banking, including more accurate client modeling, improved risk assessment and detection, and more personalized client experiences,” the release said.

BMO said the project is part of a larger effort to “responsibly” apply quantum technologies to machine learning and AI applications. Kristin Milchanowski, chief AI and quantum officer and director of the BMO Institute for Applied Artificial Intelligence & Quantum, called the announcement a milestone for BMO and the wider financial services industry.

“While we remain in the early stages of application development, these projects show how quantum computing can help solve business problems in new ways,” she said. “This work builds on years of research, collaboration and innovation focused on identifying practical applications that create value for clients, employees and shareholders.”

In the wake of recent advances in quantum computing, PYMNTS wrote earlier this year that the technology had imposed a “depreciation schedule” on encryption.

The problem, that report says, is that an attack “may be years away, but the liability already exists,” which makes quantum cybersecurity unusual when it comes to budgeting. Companies are being asked to spend now not because a control has failed, but because its anticipated lifespan has shrunk.

“The time to start thinking about migrating to quantum-resistant methods of encryption is now,” Professor Scott Aaronson, scientific advisor to StarkWare, said in a conversation hosted by PYMNTS CEO Karen Webster in February.

Cryptography embedded across applications, certificates, APIs, hardware, software libraries and third-party systems is an enterprise asset whose reliability in the future can no longer be taken for granted. Migrating it means doing an inventory of cryptographic dependencies, classifying data by confidentiality horizon, testing replacement algorithms and pressing vendors to come up with migration paths.

“That turns quantum readiness into a technology-debt problem,” the report said. “The enterprises facing the largest eventual bill may not necessarily be those with the most sensitive information. They may be those that do not know where their cryptography lives.”
